questions.q: What is the literal meaning of the word "quill" in the poem, and what does it symbolise in the context of Dogri language?
questions.a: The literal meaning of "quill" is a feather used as a pen; symbolically, it represents the Sharade script (the native writing system of Dogri) that the language has been deprived of. A wrong answer (e.g., "quill symbolises the poet's creativity") reveals the student cannot distinguish between a general poetic symbol and the specific historical-cultural symbol tied to the poem's context about script loss.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the reed's response ("Are you some sort of an accountant / With some Shah / Writing account books / Where you need a new pen / Every other day?") is ironic.
questions.a: The irony lies in the reed treating the poet's request for a quill as a trivial, repetitive clerical need, while the poet is actually engaged in a vital, urgent service to her mother tongue. A wrong answer (e.g., "It is ironic because reeds don't talk") shows the student confuses personification with irony and misses the contrast between the reed's mundane assumption and the poet's profound purpose.

questions.q: Apply the concept of situational irony to the moment when the reed cuts off its hand and gives it to the poet. What expectation is subverted?
questions.a: The expectation is that a reed (a plant) cannot voluntarily give a part of itself; the situational irony is that the reed, after complaining about the poet's demand, willingly sacrifices its "hand" (stem) to serve the same Shahni. A wrong answer (e.g., "It's ironic because the reed is a plant") merely restates the personification without identifying the subversion of the reed's earlier reluctance.

questions.q: Analyze how the symbol of the "Shahni" (the mother tongue Dogri) and the "servants" (the reed, the poet, and others) work together to develop the theme of linguistic servitude and devotion.
questions.a: The Shahni represents Dogri as a benevolent but demanding mistress; the poet and the reed are her servants, showing that both the speaker and the very tool of writing (reed/quill) are subservient to the language. This collective servitude underscores the theme that the language's survival depends on devoted service. A wrong answer (e.g., "Shahni is just a rich woman") fails to abstract the literal figure into the symbolic representation of the mother tongue.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of using irony versus symbolism in conveying the poet's anguish over the loss of the Sharade script. Which device carries more emotional weight and why?
questions.a: Symbolism carries more sustained emotional weight because the quill-as-lost-script recurs as a central motif, while irony provides sharp, momentary contrast that highlights the absurdity of the script's neglect. A good evaluation justifies this with textual evidence (e.g., the quill request frames the poem; the irony is confined to the reed's speech). A weak answer merely prefers one device without linking to the poem's specific emotional trajectory.

questions.q: Create a four-line stanza that uses both irony and symbolism to express a personal feeling about losing something culturally valuable (e.g., a dialect, a tradition, a script). Use a symbol and an ironic twist.
questions.a: A strong stanza will include a concrete symbol (e.g., a broken bangle for a lost craft) and an ironic situation (e.g., the bangle-seller laughing while the craft dies). A poor answer uses only metaphor or only irony, or fails to make the irony clear (e.g., "I lost my language / It fell in the well / Now I speak another / And all is well" – no irony, no distinct symbol).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Irony is a literary device where there is a contrast between ______ and reality, often revealing a deeper truth; symbolism is the use of an object, person, or action to represent an abstract idea beyond its literal meaning.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you ask a ______ for a pen, and he scolds you for losing the one he gave you yesterday, asking if you are an accountant who needs a new pen daily.
What is Irony? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Irony is a literary device where there is a contrast between expectation and reality, often revealing a deeper truth; symbolism is the use of an object, person, or action to represent an abstract idea beyond its literal meaning.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Irony?
questions.a: Students often think the irony in the poem is simply that a reed talks (personification) or that the poet asks a plant for a pen.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify specific instances of irony and symbolism in the poem, explain how they function together to convey the theme of linguistic deprivation, and write a structured analytical answer using textual evidence (PEEL format) suitable for board exams.
